facts.fact: AWS Emulator là công cụ giả lập cục bộ các API của AWS do chính AWS phát triển bằng ngôn ngữ Rust.
facts.quote: AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs.

facts.fact: Công cụ hoàn toàn miễn phí, chạy độc lập và không yêu cầu phải có tài khoản AWS.
facts.quote: You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee.

facts.fact: Mã nguồn chính của AWS Emulator được phát hành dưới giấy phép mã nguồn mở công cộng CC0 1.0 (Public Domain).
facts.quote: This software is licensed under the CC0 1.0 Universal (CC0-1.0) License, except the code in the `vendor/` directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0.

facts.fact: Dự án chỉ nhằm mục đích phát triển và kiểm thử, không dùng cho tải thực tế (production) hoặc kiểm thử bảo mật.
facts.quote: AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security.

facts.fact: Khi không tải (idle), bộ giả lập chỉ chiếm khoảng 160 MiB RAM trên Linux.
facts.quote: It uses about 160 MiB when idle and grows as your tests create resources.

facts.fact: Toàn bộ tài nguyên được lưu trên RAM, khi tắt tiến trình thì dữ liệu giả lập và các tệp cấu hình tạm thời sẽ bị xoá sạch.
facts.quote: The emulator stops cleanly and deletes the files that it created in ~/.aws/emulator/<port>/. It also deletes all emulated resources, because it keeps them only in memory.

facts.fact: Mặc định công cụ lắng nghe kết nối HTTPS trên địa chỉ cục bộ 127.0.0.1 cổng 9297 bằng chứng chỉ tự ký.
facts.quote: By default, the emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only your own machine can reach it.

facts.fact: Trên Linux, gói cài đặt được đặt vào thư mục /opt/aws-emulator/ và tự tạo lệnh nhị phân trong /usr/bin/.
facts.quote: The package installs the emulator in /opt/aws-emulator/ and adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so the command is on your PATH.

facts.fact: Gói cài đặt Linux được ký số bảo mật bởi AWS với mã vân tay khóa GPG chính thức.
facts.quote: The fingerprint must be 98BC F336 A3BE 53B7 34E9 67C5 2E5B F49B D940 F624. If it’s different, don’t install the package.

facts.fact: Có thể giới hạn bộ nhớ tối đa (ví dụ 2 GiB) và vô hiệu hóa swap bằng systemd-run.
facts.quote: systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=2G -p MemorySwapMax=0 aws-emulator

facts.fact: Mặc định các yêu cầu API gửi tới emulator bắt buộc phải ký bằng thuật toán SigV4 giống như AWS thật.
facts.quote: When you run AWS Emulator as a local process, by default it requires API requests to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), like AWS does.

facts.fact: Người dùng có thể tắt hoàn toàn bước xác thực chữ ký SigV4 bằng cờ --auth off.
facts.quote: To turn off signature checks, start the emulator with --auth off (-a off).

facts.fact: Tài khoản giả lập mặc định luôn có Account ID là 000000000000.
facts.quote: The emulator uses one account, 000000000000. If you reach the emulator, the output shows Account as 000000000000 and Arn as arn:aws:iam::000000000000:user/emulator.

facts.fact: Cung cấp sẵn endpoint kiểm tra tình trạng dịch vụ qua giao thức HTTPS trả về mã 200 ok.
facts.quote: The health check returns HTTP 200 with the body ok. It uses the same port as the API, over HTTPS.

facts.fact: Bắt buộc phải tắt tiêm tiền tố tên miền (host prefix injection) trong SDK để tránh gửi nhầm request vào domain không tồn tại.
facts.quote: AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION stops the AWS CLI and the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) from adding a prefix to the host name of the endpoint.

facts.fact: Cần tắt truy vấn metadata của EC2 để tránh việc SDK tự lấy nhầm thông tin đăng nhập thực khi test trên EC2.
facts.quote: AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED stops your SDK from asking the Amazon EC2 instance metadata service for credentials.

facts.fact: Mỗi phiên emulator chỉ phục vụ một AWS Region duy nhất, muốn test nhiều Region cần chạy nhiều tiến trình trên cổng khác nhau.
facts.quote: Use one Region for all your requests. To test several Regions, run one emulator for each Region.

facts.fact: Tính năng thu thập dữ liệu viễn trắc (telemetry) được bật mặc định khi khởi động.
facts.quote: AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default.

facts.fact: AWS không cung cấp sẵn Docker image đóng gói sẵn trên registry mà người dùng phải tự build từ Dockerfile.
facts.quote: We don’t publish a prebuilt image. You build one from a short Dockerfile that installs the Linux package.

facts.fact: Kho lưu trữ mã nguồn mở gốc của LocalStack trên GitHub hiện đã chuyển sang trạng thái lưu trữ (archived / read-only).
facts.quote: As part of this transition, this repository is now **archived and read-only**.

facts.fact: Kho chứa mã nguồn của AWS Emulator trên GitHub không chấp nhận Pull Request từ cộng đồng bên ngoài.
facts.quote: This repository does not take PRs.

facts.fact: Nếu tự biên dịch từ mã nguồn Rust, người dùng cần tối thiểu 100 GB dung lượng ổ cứng trống cho thư mục target/.
facts.quote: At least 100 GB of free disk for `target/`. The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added.

# AWS Emulator README

AWS Emulator is a local emulator of the AWS APIs. You use it to test your software without calling AWS, on your own machine, on a development server, or in continuous integration (CI). You don’t need an AWS account. Your requests go to the emulator, not to AWS. So you work with emulated resources instead of AWS resources. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS.

The emulator is a local program that serves an AWS API endpoint. It has no graphical interface. After you start the emulator, you set environment variables to point the AWS CLI or an AWS SDK at its endpoint. Then you run your code as usual. In embedded mode, you pass the emulator’s HTTP client to your SDK instead.

AWS Emulator is for building and testing. Don’t use it for production workloads or to test security. See [Security in AWS Emulator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/security.html).

**Documentation:** [AWS Emulator User Guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/what-is-service.html)

## Quick start

### With an AI coding agent

Install the `aws-emulator` skill, then ask your agent to set up the emulator. This needs the AWS CLI version 2.35.0 or later. See [Getting started with an AI coding agent](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/getting-started-agent.html).

```bash
aws agent-toolkit add-skill --skill-name aws-emulator --region us-east-1
```

### Server mode (CLI and any SDK)

- **Linux:** install the RPM or Debian package and run `aws-emulator`. See [Getting started on Linux](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/getting-started-linux.html).
- **Windows / macOS:** run the emulator in a container built from a short Dockerfile. See [Getting started with Docker](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/getting-started-docker.html).

Point your SDK at a running emulator by setting environment variables. See [Pointing your AWS SDK at AWS Emulator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/point-sdk-to-emulator.html).

### Embedded mode (Rust tests)

Add the emulator as a dev-dependency and run it in-process, one isolated instance per test. There is no endpoint URL, certificate, or environment variable to set. Your test wires the emulator's HTTP client straight into the SDK client. See [Getting started with embedded mode](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/getting-started-embedded.html), and [Building from source](#building-from-source) below for its build cost.

## Known issues

To see how closely each service matches AWS, check the fidelity scores published with each release on the [releases page](https://github.com/aws/aws-emulator/releases). To check whether your own project is expected to work, see [Checking whether your project works with AWS Emulator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/check-project.html).

Individual gaps are tracked in the repository's `issues/` directory. APIs and behaviors that don't work yet are under `issues/things-that-do-not-work/`, and ones that have since been fixed move to `issues/things-that-now-work/`.

## Building from source

You need this if you are modifying the emulator, running it from a checkout, or using embedded mode. Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so the prerequisites and build-cost guidance below apply to it too. Most other users install a prebuilt package instead (see [Quick start](#quick-start)). Building from source is supported on **Linux (x86_64 and aarch64)**; on Windows and macOS, use the Docker path above.

### Prerequisites

- A Rust toolchain with Cargo (install via [rustup](https://rustup.rs)).
- A C compiler, such as GCC or clang. Some dependencies build C code.
- At least 100 GB of free disk for `target/`. The workspace has one crate per AWS service, so a debug build of everything is large, and it grows as services are added.
- A multi-core machine. A cold full build compiles every service crate, so the first build takes a while; fewer cores take proportionally longer. After that, rebuilding after a change to one service is much faster.

### Build and run

```bash
cargo build -p aws-emulator-router
cargo run   -p aws-emulator-router
```

The emulator serves HTTPS on `127.0.0.1:9297` (self-signed certificate).

### Embedded mode build cost

Embedded mode compiles the emulator into your test binary, so your project's first `cargo test` builds the emulator's service crates alongside your own code. Budget a first build and `target/` on the same order as building from source above, then fast incremental builds. Recommendation: reuse one `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` across projects, cache `target/` (or use sccache) in CI, and pin the emulator to a release commit so it isn't rebuilt on every change.

## Repository layout

```
.
├── Cargo.toml              # workspace: one member per service, plus the core crates
├── services/
│   └── service-/     # ONE CRATE PER SERVICE
│       ├── smithy-model/   # .json — the Smithy model that drives the wire protocol
│       ├── build.rs        # generates the service declaration from the model
│       ├── src/
│       │   ├── service.rs  # request routing and refusal overrides
│       │   ├── state.rs    # this service's in-memory state
│       │   └── ops/        # one file per operation
│       └── tests/
├── core/
│   ├── router/             # the emulator binary: mounts every service on one endpoint
│   └── embedded/           # the in-process (embedded mode) facade
├── vendor/                 # framework crates — do not edit (replaced on update)
└── issues/                 # tracked fidelity issues
```

## Telemetry

AWS Emulator is configured to collect and report usage data to AWS, to gain insight into how AWS Emulator is used. Telemetry is on by default. AWS Emulator collects telemetry data with strict data minimization in mind, preventing identification or attribution to specific users, accounts, or organizations. Its records never include what’s in your requests or responses, your code, your credentials, or personal data. We don’t share telemetry with third parties.

For details on what is collected and how the data is handled, see [Telemetry in AWS Emulator](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emulator/latest/userguide/telemetry.html). To turn telemetry off, use one of the following options.

### Use a command-line option

Start the emulator with the `--telemetry` option (short form `-t`) set to `off`. This setting applies only to that emulator process.

```bash
aws-emulator --telemetry off
```

In a container, add `--telemetry off` after the image name in the `docker run` command.

### Use an environment variable

Set `EMULATOR_TELEMETRY` to `off` before you start the emulator. This setting applies to every emulator that you start from that shell.

`EMULATOR_TELEMETRY` accepts `on`, `true`, or `1` to turn telemetry on, and `off`, `false`, or `0` to turn it off. Values aren’t case sensitive. Any other value turns telemetry off, and the startup notice shows a warning.

```bash
export EMULATOR_TELEMETRY=off
aws-emulator
```

### Use a configuration file

To turn telemetry off for every run on a machine, add these lines to the emulator settings file, `config.toml`. The file is `~/.aws/emulator/config.toml` on Linux and macOS, and `%USERPROFILE%\.aws\emulator\config.toml` on Windows. To use a different file, set the `EMULATOR_CONFIG` environment variable to its path.

```toml
[telemetry]
enabled = false
```

### Use the embedded configuration API

In embedded mode, turn off telemetry in the options that you pass when you create the emulator.

```rust
use aws_emulator_embedded::{AwsEmulatorEmbedded, EmbeddedOptions, Telemetry};

fn main() {
    let emulator = AwsEmulatorEmbedded::new(EmbeddedOptions::default().telemetry(Telemetry::Off));
    let _http_client = emulator.http_client();
}
```

You might build a tool that includes the emulator, such as a test framework that other people run. If you do, tell your users about telemetry and give them a way to turn it off. You can also ship your tool with telemetry off.

## Reporting issues and contributing

Report bugs and fidelity gaps in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/aws/aws-emulator/issues). The most useful report names the service, the operation, your SDK and version, the request you sent, and how the response differed from real AWS. This repository does not take PRs.

## License

This software is licensed under the CC0 1.0 Universal (CC0-1.0) License, except the code in the `vendor/` directory, which is under the Apache License 2.0. See [LICENSE](LICENSE) for details, and [vendor/README.md](vendor/README.md) for the license of the code in `vendor/`.

# Overview

[LocalStack](https://localstack.cloud) is a cloud service emulator that runs in a single container on your laptop or in your CI environment. With LocalStack, you can run your AWS applications or Lambdas entirely on your local machine without connecting to a remote cloud provider! Whether you are testing complex CDK applications or Terraform configurations, or just beginning to learn about AWS services, LocalStack helps speed up and simplify your testing and development workflow.

LocalStack supports a growing number of AWS services, like AWS Lambda, S3, DynamoDB, Kinesis, SQS, SNS, and many more! The [Pro version of LocalStack](https://localstack.cloud/pricing) supports additional APIs and advanced features. You can find a comprehensive list of supported APIs on our [☑️ Feature Coverage](https://docs.localstack.cloud/user-guide/aws/feature-coverage/) page.

LocalStack also provides additional features to make your life as a cloud developer easier! Check out LocalStack's [User Guides](https://docs.localstack.cloud/user-guide/) for more information.

## Install

The quickest way to get started with LocalStack is by using the LocalStack CLI. It enables you to start and manage the LocalStack Docker container directly through your command line. Ensure that your machine has a functional [`docker` environment](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) installed before proceeding.

### Brew (macOS or Linux with Homebrew)

Install the LocalStack CLI through our [official LocalStack Brew Tap](https://github.com/localstack/homebrew-tap):

```bash
brew install localstack/tap/localstack-cli
```

### Binary download (macOS, Linux, Windows)

If Brew is not installed on your machine, you can download the pre-built LocalStack CLI binary directly:

- Visit [localstack/localstack-cli](https://github.com/localstack/localstack-cli/releases/latest) and download the latest release for your platform.
- Extract the downloaded archive to a directory included in your `PATH` variable:
  - For macOS/Linux, use the command: `sudo tar xvzf ~/Downloads/localstack-cli-*-darwin-*-onefile.tar.gz -C /usr/local/bin`

### PyPI (macOS, Linux, Windows)

LocalStack is developed using Python. To install the LocalStack CLI using `pip`, run the following command:

```bash
python3 -m pip install localstack
```

The `localstack-cli` installation enables you to run the Docker image containing the LocalStack runtime. To interact with the local AWS services, you need to install the `awslocal` CLI separately. For installation guidelines, refer to the [`awslocal` documentation](https://docs.localstack.cloud/user-guide/integrations/aws-cli/#localstack-aws-cli-awslocal).

> **Important**: Do not use `sudo` or run as `root` user. LocalStack must be installed and started entirely under a local non-root user. If you have problems with permissions in macOS High Sierra, install with `pip install --user localstack`

## Running

You can run LocalStack through the following options:

- [LocalStack CLI](https://docs.localstack.cloud/getting-started/installation/#localstack-cli)
- [Docker](https://docs.localstack.cloud/getting-started/installation/#docker)

## Install

```console
$ pip install 'moto[ec2,s3,all]'
```

## In a nutshell

Moto is a library that allows your tests to easily mock out AWS Services.

Imagine you have the following python code that you want to test:

```python
import boto3

class MyModel:
    def __init__(self, name, value):
        self.name = name
        self.value = value

    def save(self):
        s3 = boto3.client("s3", region_name="us-east-1")
        s3.put_object(Bucket="mybucket", Key=self.name, Body=self.value)
```

Take a minute to think how you would have tested that in the past.

Now see how you could test it with Moto:

```python
import boto3
from moto import mock_aws
from mymodule import MyModel

@mock_aws
def test_my_model_save():
    conn = boto3.resource("s3", region_name="us-east-1")
    # We need to create the bucket since this is all in Moto's 'virtual' AWS account
    conn.create_bucket(Bucket="mybucket")
    model_instance = MyModel("steve", "is awesome")
    model_instance.save()
    body = conn.Object("mybucket", "steve").get()["Body"].read().decode("utf-8")
    assert body == "is awesome"
```

With the decorator wrapping the test, all the calls to s3 are automatically mocked out. The mock keeps track of the state of the buckets and keys.

For a full list of which services and features are covered, please see our [implementation coverage](https://github.com/getmoto/moto/blob/master/IMPLEMENTATION_COVERAGE.md).

On Linux, you install AWS Emulator as a native package and run it as a local process. The package installs the emulator in /opt/aws-emulator/ and adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so the command is on your PATH.

First, check what you need in Setting up AWS Emulator.

To install AWS Emulator

Download and install the package for your system. The commands differ by package type and processor.

RPM package (x86_64)

sudo dnf install -y https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm

RPM package (aarch64)

sudo dnf install -y https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator-aarch64.rpm

Debian package (amd64)

curl -fsSLo aws-emulator.deb https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator_amd64.deb
sudo apt-get install -y ./aws-emulator.deb

Debian package (arm64)

curl -fsSLo aws-emulator.deb https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator_arm64.deb
sudo apt-get install -y ./aws-emulator.deb

On Amazon Linux 2, use yum for the RPM commands on this page.

The package also installs the license and notice files for AWS Emulator.

These commands install the latest release. To install a specific version, see Finding and installing a specific version. To check the package before you install it, see To verify the package before you install it (optional).

Confirm the installation. The command prints the version. For what it shows, see Version numbers.

aws-emulator -v
To verify the package before you install it (optional)

AWS signs each package. The signature is in a file next to the package, with the same name plus .sig. To check that a package comes from AWS and wasn’t changed, verify it before you install it. You need GnuPG (gpg), which most Linux distributions include.

Download the package and its signature file. The following example uses the RPM package for x86_64. For another package, change the file name in PACKAGE_FILE.

PACKAGE_FILE=aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm
curl -fsSLO https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/$PACKAGE_FILE
curl -fsSLO https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/$PACKAGE_FILE.sig

Import the public key.

curl -fsSLo aws-publishing.asc https://downloads.aws.com/keys/gpg/current.asc
gpg --import aws-publishing.asc

Check the fingerprint of the key.

gpg --fingerprint ssm-publishing@amazon.com

The fingerprint must be 98BC F336 A3BE 53B7 34E9 67C5 2E5B F49B D940 F624. If it’s different, don’t install the package.

Verify the signature.

gpg --verify $PACKAGE_FILE.sig $PACKAGE_FILE

The output includes Good signature from "SSM Publishing <ssm-publishing@amazon.com>". It also warns that the key isn’t certified with a trusted signature. You can ignore this warning, because you checked the fingerprint. If the output says BAD signature, delete both files, and don’t install the package.

Install the file that you verified.

RPM package

sudo dnf install -y ./$PACKAGE_FILE

Debian package

sudo apt-get install -y ./$PACKAGE_FILE
To start and stop AWS Emulator

Start the emulator.

aws-emulator

The emulator keeps running in that terminal. The startup line of its log gives the address and port that it serves on, and you can rely on it in scripts. For what the log contains, see Output.

By default, the emulator serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only your own machine can reach it. For all options, see AWS Emulator command reference.

In another terminal, set the environment variables for your SDK, and then run your code. For example, set AWS_CONFIG_FILE to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/config and AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials. For the full list, see To point your SDK at a local emulator. For Java, also see To trust the emulator certificate in Java.

To stop the emulator, press Ctrl+C in its terminal, or send the process a SIGTERM signal. The emulator stops cleanly and deletes the files that it created in ~/.aws/emulator/<port>/. It also deletes all emulated resources, because it keeps them only in memory.

To use a different port

If another program already uses port 9297, the emulator can’t start. For the error that it prints, see When the port is in use. To fix this, choose another port when you start the emulator.

To use a specific port, run aws-emulator -p <port>. For example, run aws-emulator -p 9300.

To let the operating system choose a free port, run aws-emulator -p 0. Then read the port from the endpoint_url field of the startup line in the log.

You can run several emulators side by side. Give each one a different port with -p, or use -p 0 for each one. Each emulator keeps its own files in ~/.aws/emulator/<port>/, and its own resources. When you set the environment variables for an emulator, use that emulator’s port in each one.

To limit the memory of the emulator on Linux

The emulator keeps emulated resources in memory. It uses about 160 MiB when idle and grows as your tests create resources. You can cap its memory with a systemd scope. This needs a systemd user session on cgroup v2. Amazon Linux 2 and many containers don’t have one. On those systems, use Docker instead, as described in To run AWS Emulator in a container.

Start the emulator with the following systemd-run command. It sets a limit of 2 GiB, and MemorySwapMax=0 keeps the emulator out of swap.

systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=2G -p MemorySwapMax=0 aws-emulator

The emulator runs in the foreground, as it does without the limit.

If the emulator goes over the limit, the kernel stops it with exit code 137. You lose the emulated resources. To start again with empty state, run the command again.

To uninstall AWS Emulator

Stop any running emulator.

Remove the package.

RPM systems

sudo dnf remove -y aws-emulator

Debian systems

sudo apt-get remove -y aws-emulator

(Optional) Delete the files the emulator keeps in your home directory.

Important

This command deletes all the files that the emulator keeps in your home directory. Do this only when you’re done with the emulator.

rm -rf ~/.aws/emulator

To use AWS Emulator, you configure the AWS CLI or your AWS SDK to send requests to the emulator instead of to AWS. When you run the emulator as a local process (Linux or Docker), you set environment variables. When you run it embedded in Rust tests, you replace the SDK HTTP client. For embedded mode, see Getting started with embedded mode.

How the emulator handles credentials and HTTPS

When you run AWS Emulator as a local process, by default it requires API requests to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), like AWS does. Signature checks protect you from requests that a web page or another local program sends to the emulator without your knowledge. For which keys the emulator accepts and the errors that it returns, see Credentials and authentication. For how this protects your machine, see What we do.

When the emulator starts, it generates a new access key ID and secret access key. It writes them, a config file for your SDK, and its certificate (ca.pem, and truststore.p12 for Java) to a subdirectory of ~/.aws/emulator/ named for its port, for example ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. The keys work only with this run of the emulator. For what each file contains and when it’s deleted, see Local files.

To turn off signature checks, start the emulator with --auth off (-a off). The emulator then serves every request and doesn’t write the emulator_credentials file. Before you use this option, see What you do.

To point your SDK at a local emulator

Start the emulator. For more information, see Getting started with AWS Emulator.

In the shell where you run your code, set the following environment variables. If you use a port other than 9297, replace 9297 in each value.

macOS and Linux

export AWS_ENDPOINT_URL=https://127.0.0.1:9297
export AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/emulator_credentials
export AWS_CONFIG_FILE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/config
export AWS_CA_BUNDLE=~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem
export AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED=true
export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
export AWS_REGION=us-east-1
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=us-east-1

Windows PowerShell

$env:AWS_ENDPOINT_URL = "https://127.0.0.1:9297"
$env:AWS_SHARED_CREDENTIALS_FILE = "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator\9297\emulator_credentials"
$env:AWS_CONFIG_FILE = "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator\9297\config"
$env:AWS_CA_BUNDLE = "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator\9297\ca.pem"
$env:AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED = "true"
$env:AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION = "true"
$env:AWS_REGION = "us-east-1"
$env:AWS_DEFAULT_REGION = "us-east-1"

AWS_EC2_METADATA_DISABLED stops your SDK from asking the Amazon EC2 instance metadata service for credentials. This keeps your SDK from using real credentials when you test on an EC2 instance.

AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION stops the AWS CLI and the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) from adding a prefix to the host name of the endpoint. For other SDKs, see Host names that your SDK changes.

Setting AWS_CONFIG_FILE replaces your own AWS config file for that shell. Settings that you keep there, such as retry or Amazon S3 settings, don’t apply while you test against the emulator. The emulator writes its config file again each time it starts, so don’t add your settings to it. Instead, copy the file, add your settings to the copy, and set AWS_CONFIG_FILE to the copy. If you change the emulator’s port, make the copy again.

Use one Region for all your requests. To test several Regions, run one emulator for each Region. For more information, see Limitations.

AWS_CA_BUNDLE makes the AWS CLI, Boto3, and the AWS SDK for Go trust the emulator’s certificate. It also works when the emulator runs in Docker, where the certificate path in config is a path in the container.

Unset any variables that can supply real AWS credentials. Environment variables take precedence over the credentials file. If you leave them set, your SDK signs requests with your real credentials, and the emulator rejects those requests.

macOS and Linux

unset AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY AWS_SESSION_TOKEN AWS_PROFILE

Windows PowerShell

Remove-Item Env:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, Env:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, Env:AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, Env:AWS_PROFILE -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

If your SDK doesn’t read AWS_CA_BUNDLE, set the variable for your language from the table in Trusting the emulator certificate in each SDK.

(Optional) Check that the emulator is ready. The health check returns HTTP 200 with the body ok. It uses the same port as the API, over HTTPS.

curl --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health

In a script, you can wait for the emulator before you run your tests. The following loop tries once per second, for up to 30 seconds.

for i in $(seq 30); do
  curl -sf --cacert ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem https://127.0.0.1:9297/__admin/health && break
  sleep 1
done

Run your code. Your SDK reads the variables that you set, so your code needs no endpoint or credentials. For example, the following Python code lists the Amazon S3 buckets in the emulator.

import boto3

s3 = boto3.client("s3")
print(s3.list_buckets()["Buckets"])
Important

Make sure that your tests send requests to the emulator, not to AWS. If AWS_ENDPOINT_URL isn’t set in the shell that runs your tests, your code calls AWS with whatever credentials it finds. Set the variables in the same script that runs your tests, and don’t keep real credentials in the environment of your test jobs.

Host names that your SDK changes

The emulator serves all services on one endpoint, https://127.0.0.1:9297. For some requests, your SDK changes the host name of the endpoint before it sends the request. A request that goes to a different host name doesn’t reach the emulator.

Host prefixes – For some operations, the SDK adds a prefix to the host name. For example, it adds data- for AWS Cloud Map DiscoverInstances, sync- for AWS Step Functions StartSyncExecution, and stream- for Amazon CloudWatch Logs StartLiveTail. The request then goes to a host such as data-127.0.0.1, which doesn’t exist. To prevent this, turn off host prefix injection in your SDK, as shown in the following table.

Amazon S3 – The endpoint is an IP address. So your SDK puts the bucket name in the path of each Amazon S3 request, not in the host name. The emulator doesn’t accept requests that put the bucket name in the host name. Keep 127.0.0.1 in AWS_ENDPOINT_URL. If you use localhost instead, the AWS SDKs for JavaScript, Java, and Go put the bucket name in the host name by default.

Amazon S3 Control – Your SDK always puts your account ID in the host name of an Amazon S3 Control request, such as 000000000000.127.0.0.1. You can’t turn this off, so Amazon S3 Control requests don’t reach the emulator.

SDK	How to turn off host prefix injection

AWS CLI

	

Set AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION to true.

AWS SDK for Python (Boto3)

	

Set AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION to true, or create the client with Config(inject_host_prefix=False).

AWS SDK for JavaScript v3

	

Create the client with disableHostPrefix: true.

AWS SDK for Java 2.x

	

Set SdkAdvancedClientOption.DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION to true in the client override configuration.

Set AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION only in the shell where you use the emulator. On AWS, operations that use a host prefix fail when the variable is set. For example, Cloud Map DiscoverInstances returns UnknownOperationException.

The following example uses the AWS CLI to find the instances of a Cloud Map service. Without AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION, the AWS CLI sends the request to data-127.0.0.1, and the request fails.

$ aws servicediscovery discover-instances --namespace-name my-namespace --service-name my-service
Could not connect to the endpoint URL: "https://data-127.0.0.1:9297/"

With AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION set to true, the request reaches the emulator, and the emulator returns the instances that you registered.

$ export AWS_DISABLE_HOST_PREFIX_INJECTION=true
$ aws servicediscovery discover-instances --namespace-name my-namespace --service-name my-service \
    --query 'Instances[].{InstanceId: InstanceId, Attributes: Attributes}'
[
    {
        "InstanceId": "my-instance",
        "Attributes": {
            "AWS_INSTANCE_IPV4": "10.0.0.1"
        }
    }
]
To check that you’re using the emulator

To confirm that your shell sends requests to the emulator, run the following command.

aws sts get-caller-identity

The emulator uses one account, 000000000000. If you reach the emulator, the output shows Account as 000000000000 and Arn as arn:aws:iam::000000000000:user/emulator. If you see your own account ID, your requests go to AWS. Check the variables in To point your SDK at a local emulator.

Trusting the emulator certificate in each SDK

The emulator serves HTTPS with its own certificate. The AWS CLI and some SDKs read the certificate from AWS_CA_BUNDLE, which you set in To point your SDK at a local emulator. Others need an extra setting. The following table lists the setting for each client.

Client	Extra setting for HTTPS

AWS CLI version 2

	

None. Reads AWS_CA_BUNDLE.

AWS SDK for Python (Boto3)

	

None. Reads AWS_CA_BUNDLE.

AWS SDK for Go v2

	

None. Reads AWS_CA_BUNDLE.

AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 (Node.js)

	

NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS set to the path of ca.pem, for example ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem

AWS SDK for Java 2.x

	

JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS set to use the emulator’s truststore.p12. For more information, see To trust the emulator certificate in Java.

AWS SDK for Rust

	

SSL_CERT_FILE set to the path of ca.pem, for example ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem

AWS SDK for .NET

	

SSL_CERT_FILE set to the path of ca.pem, for example ~/.aws/emulator/9297/ca.pem

The emulator creates a new certificate each time it starts. Settings that point to the path of ca.pem or truststore.p12 keep working. If you copy or import the certificate, repeat that step after each start.

On Windows, you might need to import ca.pem into the Windows certificate store, depending on your SDK.

If your code must also reach other HTTPS servers, including AWS, see Reaching the emulator and other HTTPS servers from one process.

To trust the emulator certificate in Java

Java doesn’t read ca.pem. Instead, the emulator writes the same certificate to truststore.p12, a PKCS12 trust store without a password, in the same folder as ca.pem. To use it, point the Java virtual machine (JVM) at it. For example, set JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS in the shell that runs your tests. If you use a port other than 9297, replace 9297 in the path.

macOS and Linux

export JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=$HOME/.aws/emulator/9297/truststore.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreType=PKCS12"

Windows PowerShell

$env:JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS = "-Djavax.net.ssl.trustStore=$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator\9297\truststore.p12 -Djavax.net.ssl.trustStoreType=PKCS12"

Every JVM that you start from that shell reads JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, including build tools such as Gradle and Maven. To limit the setting to your tests, pass the same options to the test JVM only. For example, use jvmArgs in a Gradle test task, or argLine in the Maven Surefire plugin.

This trust store replaces the JVM’s default trust store, so calls to other HTTPS servers, including AWS, fail with PKIX path building failed. To reach both, see Reaching the emulator and other HTTPS servers from one process.

Reaching the emulator and other HTTPS servers from one process

Most of the settings in Trusting the emulator certificate in each SDK replace the certificates that your code trusts by default, so your code then trusts only the emulator. This applies to ca_bundle, AWS_CA_BUNDLE, SSL_CERT_FILE, and the Java trust store. NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS in Node.

On any system that runs Docker, including Windows and macOS, you can run the emulator in a Docker container. We don’t publish a prebuilt image. You build one from a short Dockerfile that installs the Linux package.

First, install Docker. For the other prerequisites, see Setting up AWS Emulator.

To build the AWS Emulator image

In an empty directory, create a file named Dockerfile with the following content.

FROM public.ecr.aws/amazonlinux/amazonlinux:2023-minimal
ADD https://downloads.aws.com/aws-emulator/packages/aws-emulator/LTS/latest/aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm /tmp/aws-emulator.rpm
RUN rpm -i /tmp/aws-emulator.rpm && rm /tmp/aws-emulator.rpm \
    && mkdir -p /home/emulator && chown 1000 /home/emulator
USER 1000
ENV HOME=/home/emulator
EXPOSE 9297
ENTRYPOINT ["aws-emulator", "-b", "0.0.0.0"]

On computers with Apple silicon or other Arm processors, use the Arm package instead. In the ADD line, replace aws-emulator-x86_64.rpm with aws-emulator-aarch64.rpm.

The -b 0.0.0.0 option makes the emulator listen on all addresses inside the container, so Docker can forward its port. The docker run command in the next procedure opens the port only to your own machine.

Build the image.

docker build -t aws-emulator .
To run AWS Emulator in a container

Create the directory that the container shares with your machine. On Linux, if you skip this step, Docker makes the directory owned by root, and your SDK can’t read it.

macOS and Linux

mkdir -p ~/.aws/emulator

Windows PowerShell

New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator"

Start the container.

macOS and Linux

PORT=9297
docker run --rm --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g -p 127.0.0.1:$PORT:$PORT \
  -e HOME="$HOME" -v "$HOME/.aws/emulator:$HOME/.aws/emulator" \
  aws-emulator -p $PORT

Windows PowerShell

$port = 9297
docker run --rm --memory=2g --memory-swap=2g -p "127.0.0.1:${port}:${port}" `
  -v "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator:/home/emulator/.aws/emulator" `
  aws-emulator -p $port

The -v option lets your SDK read the credentials and certificate that the emulator creates. It also keeps the telemetry ID between runs, so each run isn’t counted as a new install. On Linux, also add --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" after docker run so the files belong to you. To turn off telemetry in the container, see Turning telemetry off.

On macOS and Linux, -e HOME makes the emulator use the same paths in the container as on your computer. So the paths in its config file and startup line are correct on your computer. On Windows, they’re paths in the container.

The --memory and --memory-swap options limit the emulator to 2 gibibytes (GiB) of memory, with no swap. If the container goes over the limit, it stops with exit code 137, and you lose the emulated resources.

The startup message shows paths inside the container, such as /home/emulator/.aws/emulator/config.toml. Because of the -v option, that file is config.toml in the .aws/emulator folder that you mounted. Edit it there, if needed.

Use -p 127.0.0.1:9297:9297, not -p 9297:9297. The short form opens the emulator to your whole network. Other computers could then reach it.

To pass other emulator options, add them at the end of the command. For all options, see AWS Emulator command reference.

In another terminal, set the environment variables for your SDK, as shown in To point your SDK at a local emulator.

Run your code.

To stop the emulator, press Ctrl+C in its terminal. The emulator deletes its files in ~/.aws/emulator/<port>/, and Docker removes the container. You lose the emulated resources, because the emulator keeps them in memory.

To use another port, change PORT ($port in PowerShell). The command uses the port on both sides of Docker’s -p option and in the emulator’s -p option. They must match, because the emulator writes its port into the files that it creates.

To run several emulators at the same time, run the command in a separate terminal for each one, with a different port. Then use that emulator’s port in the environment variables for your SDK.

To keep each emulator’s credentials and certificate, change the port in all three places. If you change only the port on your computer, as in -p 127.0.0.1:9300:9297, the containers write to the same subdirectory of ~/.aws/emulator. They then replace and delete each other’s files.

Don’t use the emulator’s -p 0 option in a container. Docker can’t forward a port that the emulator picks when it starts.

To remove the AWS Emulator image

Stop each emulator that’s running. Press Ctrl+C in its terminal.

Remove the image.

docker image rm aws-emulator

(Optional) Delete the shared directory.

Important

This step deletes all the files that the emulator keeps in your home directory. Do this only when you’re done with the emulator.

macOS and Linux

rm -rf ~/.aws/emulator

Windows PowerShell

Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.aws\emulator"
